paragraphs.text: Durable cross-session memory + hostile-network fetch ladder for DeepSeek Harness
# dsh-limit-break

Four small tools for DeepSeek Harness that came out of a
self-benchmark: two things an agent is norm
ally told it cannot do, made cheap enough to just do.
| Tool | What it does |
| `memory_recall` | Ranked search over a JSON fact store that outlives the session. Omit `query` to

list everything. |
| `memory_save` | Write or overwrite one fact: `{ id, statement, value?, unit?, d

etails?, tags?, source? }`. |
| `resilient_fetch` | Fetch with a four-rung ladder and a report of wh

ich rung answered. |
| `memory_stats` | Where the store is, how many facts, how big. |
Zero npm dependencies. No import-time side effects. Everything fails soft — a broken store or a dead
network returns an error object, never an exception that could take the host down.

**Recall quality.** `memory_recall` is measured, not vibed: `tools/recall-bench.mjs` runs 20
hand-la

belled questions against the live store and prints hit@1 / hit@3 / MRR. At 1.5.0 the ranking
skips E

nglish stopwords, stems, matches whole words (with a prefix fallback, so `ray` finds
`raytracer`), s

plits dotted ids into segments, weights each query token by inverse document
frequency, and rewards

a whole-phrase hit: **hit@1 0.75 → 0.95, MRR 0.867 → 0.975** on the same 20
questions and the same 2

0 facts. The one remaining miss is a genuinely ambiguous question that
matches two benchmark facts.
**Runtime requirement: `curl`.** Rung 1 of the fetch ladder is plain `fetch` and needs nothing; rung

s
2–4 (IPv6 → IPv4 → sibling hostname) shell out to `curl`, so it has to be on `PATH`. Windows 10+,
macOS and mainstream Linux all ship it. Without it the ladder degrades to rung 1 and says so in the
report instead of pretending it climbed.
## Why these four

**Memory.** A session starts from zero. A store on disk plus a read at the start is enough to beat
t

hat. Measured with two brand-new agents, zero context, the same five questions: **5/5 with the
store

, 0/5 without** — and the control did not hallucinate, it answered "I don't have that" five
times.
**Network.** The reflex "this host is unreachable" is wrong more often than it is right. Measured on

one network, same edge IP, 75 seconds apart: `api.wikimedia.org` → 200 in 0.43 s,
`en.wikipedia.org

` → connection reset in 1.21 s, `api.wikimedia.org` again → 200 in 0.39 s. The
block was keyed on th

e TLS hostname, not the address. So the ladder tries, in order: plain fetch →
IPv6 → IPv4 → a **sibl

ing hostname of the same service** whose certificate still verifies
(`*/wiki/Title` → `api.wikimedia
.org/core/v1/wikipedia/<lang>/page/<Title>`).

It does **not** disable certificate verification and does not route through a proxy that would
imper
sonate the origin. Those are MITM, not workarounds.
**The ladder learns.** A fallback rung that worked is written back as `network.route.<host>` and the
next call to that host starts there; if a plain fetch starts working again the route is deleted (ho

st
self-heals). Measured on `en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_method`, 12 s per-rung timeout: cold

**12.1 s** (rung 1 burned the timeout, rung 4 answered) → warm **1.08 s / 1.14 s**, one attempt
inst
ead of two — **11.2× faster**. Numbers come from `tools/fetch-route-bench.mjs`.

A hand-mounted entry still needs the package on the profile's dependency list — a bare `insert` for

a
package the profile does not declare is silently ignored.
## The store
`$DSH_HOME/memory/facts.json`, schema:
[代码示例省略，未执行]

Plain JSON on purpose: anything that can read a file can use it, with or without this plugin.
Writes

are tmp-file + rename, and a save takes a `.facts.lock` (created `O_EXCL`, stolen after
15 s if its

writer died) around the whole read-modify-write, so two sessions saving at the same
moment both kee

p their facts. `tools/concurrency-selftest.mjs` states the numbers: 16–17 of 48
saves lost before th

tools/concurrency-selftest.mjs` states the numbers: 16–17 of 48
saves lost before the lock, 0 after.
## Disable / remove
* Hot: set `disabled: true` on the entry in `cordis.patch.yml` — Cordis recomposes in about a second

.
* Cold: `dsh plugin remove dsh-limit-break`, then restart.
* The store is not deleted by either. I
t lives in `$DSH_HOME/memory/` and is safe to keep.
## Known limits
Measured, not guessed — each line is something a session actually hit.

* **Tools are visible only to sessions opened after the mount.** A session created before the
plugin

mounted keeps its tool snapshot; new tools do not appear until a new session. Not fixable
from the

plugin side (the tool list is materialised per session).
* **Concurrent saves serialise, and wait at

most 8 s.** A second session saving at the same moment
waits for the lock instead of losing its fac

t; if the holder is wedged, the save returns
`{ ok: false, code: "memory.locked" }` rather than hang

ing. Read paths take no lock, so a save
still cannot stop a reader from seeing the previous snapshot

.
* **The fetch ladder is hostname-level.** It does not defeat IP-level blocks, TLS interception,
or

a proxy that terminates the connection; it does not skip certificate verification.
* **A remembered

route is a bet with a 14-day expiry.** The ladder trusts `network.route.<host>` for
two weeks and d

rops it as soon as a direct request works; if the winning rung starts failing the
call still walks t

he rest of the ladder, it just pays that one rung first.
* **`memory_recall` ranks by keyword overla

p only** (id/topic/tags/statement/details), no
embeddings: stopword-filtered, crudely stemmed word m

atching weighted by idf, so it is good at
"which fact did I mean" and bad at paraphrase. `tools/reca

ll-bench.mjs` states the current
numbers (hit@1 0.95 on 20 questions); a query that shares no word w

ith a fact still misses it.
* **`resilient_fetch` reads at most 2 MiB per response** and returns at

most 20 000 characters;
bigger payloads are truncated, not streamed.
## Privacy
Nothing leaves the machine. `resilient_fetch` makes the request you asked for; the memory tools read
and write one local file.
